canonicalExplanation.summary: Native HTML elements come with **built-in behaviour**: a `<button>` is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, is announced as a button, and works with forms. ARIA (`role`, `aria-*`) only changes what assistive technology is **told** — it adds no behaviour. So the first rule of ARIA is: **use the native element if one exists**. A `div role="button"` still needs tabindex, key handling and styling for focus — all of which a button gives you free.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A teammate builds a "Save" control as `<div role="button" onclick="save()">`. A screen reader calls it a button — but pressing Enter or Space does nothing, and Tab skips it. The label promises a button; the behaviour doesn't deliver. A button element triggers an action and works with Enter and Space without a custom keydown implementation. In this lesson you'll replace unnecessary ARIA or generic clickable elements with native HTML controls.

sections.heading: Bad ARIA is worse than none

includes: Replace clickable divs and spans with button, a and input.
Remove redundant or harmful ARIA and use ARIA only where native HTML can't express meaning.

outcomes: Replace unnecessary ARIA or generic clickable elements with native HTML controls.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A clickable div with role=button is fully equivalent to button without any other code.
misconceptions.correction: role=button only changes how the element is announced. Focusability, Enter and Space activation, disabled state and form behaviour must be added by hand; a native button provides them all.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "A real button for free", which behaviours did the div lack?

analogy.example: ARIA is like **putting a "Door" sign on a wall**: people now expect a door, but it still won't open. A native element is an actual door, with handle and hinges included.
limitations: Signs on real doors (aria-expanded) can add useful info.
A wrong sign (bad aria-label) misleads more than no sign.

remediation.explanation: For every role or aria-* attribute ask: **Is there a native element that already means this?** If yes, use it and delete the ARIA. If no, keep minimal ARIA and add the behaviour it promises.

recap.summary: To replace unnecessary ARIA or generic clickable elements, use native HTML controls — button, a, input, nav — which include focus, keyboard and semantics. ARIA only changes announcements; use it to fill gaps native HTML can't express, never to fake controls.
